questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: Impulses with a duration of less than 10 ms, used for stimulating normal (innervated) muscle, are classified as having:

options.A: A long duration, termed interrupted direct current
options.B: A short duration, of the faradic type
options.C: No classification exists for pulse duration
options.D: A duration only used for denervated muscle

questions.explanation: Impulses of less than 10 ms duration are classed as short duration and are of the faradic type, used to stimulate normal innervated muscle via its motor nerve, typically repeated at a high rate of 50-100 per second.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: Impulses with a duration of MORE than 10 ms, often termed interrupted (or modified) direct current, are specifically used to stimulate:

options.A: Normal, innervated muscle via the motor nerve
options.B: Denervated muscle, where the muscle fibres must be stimulated directly (no functioning motor nerve)

questions.explanation: Long-duration impulses (>10 ms), termed interrupted or modified direct current, are used for denervated muscles — since there is no functioning motor nerve, the muscle fibres must be stimulated directly, and these impulses are repeated far less frequently than faradic-type currents (e.g. a 100 ms impulse might be repeated only about 30 times per minute).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: A faradic-type current is best defined as:

options.B: A short-duration interrupted direct current with a pulse duration of 0.1-1 ms and a frequency of 50-100 Hz
options.C: A current only used for denervated muscle
options.D: A current with pulse durations always exceeding 100 ms

questions.explanation: A faradic-type current is a short-duration interrupted direct current with a pulse duration of 0.1-1 ms and a frequency of 50-100 Hz — modern electronic stimulators reproduce the same physiological effects as the original faradic coil, just via a different circuit mechanism.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Faradic-Type Current

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: Faradic-type currents are typically 'surged' for treatment purposes. What is the purpose of surging the current?

options.A: To reduce the total treatment time
options.B: To produce a near-normal tetanic-like contraction and relaxation of the muscle, by gradually increasing then decreasing the intensity of successive impulses
options.C: To eliminate the need for any electrodes
options.D: To convert the current into direct current permanently

questions.explanation: Surging gradually increases the intensity of successive impulses to a peak, then lets it fall (suddenly or gradually), mimicking a more natural, near-normal tetanic muscle contraction and relaxation cycle rather than an abrupt on/off stimulus.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Modified Faradic Currents

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When an electrical current stimulates a nerve fibre, the surface of the plasma membrane nearer the cathode becomes:

options.B: More negative relative to the opposite surface, which can reduce the resting potential difference across the membrane on the cathode side and initiate an impulse if it falls enough for sodium permeability to increase
options.D: Permanently depolarised with no possibility of returning to rest

questions.explanation: The membrane surface nearer the cathode becomes more negative. On the side of the nerve nearer the cathode, this additional charge is of opposite polarity to the resting membrane potential, reducing the potential difference (PD) across it — if the PD falls enough for the membrane to become permeable to sodium ions, an impulse is initiated.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Mechanism of Nerve Stimulation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: For a RISING (increasing) current applied over a superficial nerve, which electrode is more effective at initiating a nerve impulse, and why is the active electrode typically connected to it?

options.A: The anode, because it requires less current overall
options.B: The cathode, because it produces contraction of innervated muscle with less current than is required at the anode
options.C: Neither electrode has any different effect
options.D: The anode always requires less current than the cathode

questions.explanation: For a rising current, the cathode is more effective at initiating a nerve impulse than the anode. This is why the active electrode is conventionally connected to the cathode — it produces contraction of innervated muscle using less current than would be needed if the anode were used as the active electrode.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Mechanism of Nerve Stimulation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: 'Accommodation' in nerve physiology refers to the phenomenon whereby:

options.A: A nerve becomes permanently unresponsive after any stimulation
options.B: The nerve adapts to a constant current over time, so that an unvarying (unchanging) current becomes ineffective at initiating an impulse
options.C: Muscle fibres physically move position to avoid the electrode
options.D: Only denervated muscle can show accommodation

questions.explanation: Accommodation is the nerve's adaptation to a constant, unvarying current flow through a mechanism not fully understood — as a result, a current that does not change is not effective at initiating a nerve impulse, which is why intermittent or varying currents are needed for electrical stimulation.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Accommodation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: Because of accommodation, which type of current change is MORE effective at initiating a nerve impulse: a sudden change, or a gradual one?

options.A: A sudden change in current is more effective than a gradual one
options.B: A gradual change is always more effective
options.C: Both are exactly equally effective in all cases
options.D: Neither a sudden nor gradual change can ever initiate an impulse

questions.explanation: Because the nerve accommodates (adapts) to slowly changing conditions, a current that rises or falls suddenly is more effective at initiating an impulse than one that changes gradually, since gradual change gives the nerve time to accommodate before the threshold is reached.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Accommodation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: While a rising current initiates an impulse most effectively at the cathode, a FALL in current (when it occurs) is more effective at initiating an impulse at which electrode?

options.C: Neither electrode is affected by a falling current

questions.explanation: A fall in current is less effective overall at initiating an impulse than a rise, but when it does have an effect, it is the anode side of the nerve that is affected — so the anode produces greater stimulation than the cathode specifically in response to a falling current, the reverse of the pattern seen with a rising current.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Accommodation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: In a practical setup for stimulating the quadriceps with a faradic-type current, where is the indifferent (larger) electrode typically placed, per Clayton's described technique?

options.A: Over the femoral nerve in the femoral triangle
options.B: Directly over the motor points of the quadriceps only, with no separate indifferent electrode

questions.explanation: In the classic technique for faradic stimulation of the quadriceps, one electrode and pad is placed over the femoral nerve in the femoral triangle and secured with a sandbag or bandage, while the other (active) electrode pad is placed across the motor points of the quadriceps.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When beginning faradic stimulation of a muscle group, what is the recommended approach to intensity?

options.A: Start immediately at maximal tolerable intensity
options.B: Give several gentle contractions first to allow the patient to become accustomed to the current, then gradually increase intensity
options.C: Intensity should never be increased throughout the treatment
options.D: Intensity is irrelevant to the treatment outcome

questions.explanation: The recommended approach is to give the patient several gentle contractions first to allow them to become accustomed to the current, then gradually increase the intensity until a strong contraction is achieved — not starting at a high, potentially uncomfortable intensity immediately.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: As the frequency of repeated electrical stimuli to a motor nerve increases beyond about 20 Hz, what happens to the muscle's contraction pattern?

options.B: There is no longer time for complete relaxation between contractions, producing partial tetany
options.C: Contraction strength decreases progressively to zero
options.D: The muscle contracts only once regardless of how many stimuli are given

questions.explanation: At low stimulation frequencies (e.g. 1 per second), each stimulus produces an isolated twitch with complete relaxation between contractions. As frequency increases, the relaxation period shortens; beyond about 20 Hz there is no longer time for complete relaxation between contractions, producing partial tetany.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Frequency of Stimulation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: At what approximate stimulation frequency does a muscle contraction become fully tetanic, with no perceptible relaxation between successive contractions?

options.D: Frequency has no relationship to tetany

questions.explanation: As stimulation frequency increases beyond 20 Hz, partial tetany develops; further increases progressively reduce relaxation until, at frequencies over 60 Hz, there is no perceptible relaxation between contractions and the response is fully tetanic.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Frequency of Stimulation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When a MOTOR nerve is electrically stimulated, why does only the downward-travelling (efferent) impulse produce a muscle contraction, while the upward-travelling impulse has no motor effect?

options.A: The upward-travelling impulse is unable to pass the first synapse, since it is travelling in the wrong (antidromic) direction
options.B: The upward-travelling impulse travels faster and arrives too early to have any effect
options.C: Motor nerves cannot conduct impulses in more than one direction under any circumstance
options.D: Only the upward-travelling impulse reaches the muscle

questions.explanation: Stimulating a nerve fibre initiates impulses travelling simultaneously in both directions from the stimulation point. For a motor nerve, the upward (antidromic) impulse cannot pass the first synapse it encounters travelling the 'wrong' way, so it has no effect, while the downward (orthodromic) impulse reaches the muscle normally and causes contraction.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Nerve Stimulation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When faradic-type current is applied directly over an innervated muscle, maximum contraction response is generally obtained by stimulating at the:

options.B: Motor point — where the main nerve enters the muscle (or, for deep muscles, where it emerges from under more superficial muscles)
options.C: Muscle belly midpoint, regardless of nerve entry

questions.explanation: The motor point — the point at which the main nerve supply enters the muscle, or for deeply placed muscles, the point where the nerve emerges from under overlying superficial muscles — is where maximum contraction response is typically obtained with electrical stimulation.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Nerve Stimulation

questions.question: In a three-pin mains plug, the earth pin is made longer and thicker than the live and neutral pins so that:

options.A: It prevents the plug from being inserted the wrong way round only
options.B: It connects last so that the live pin is always energised first
options.C: It carries the main treatment current to the patient
options.D: It connects first when plugged in and disconnects last when removed

questions.explanation: The longer, thicker earth pin makes contact before the live and neutral pins and breaks last, so the metal casing is earthed whenever the apparatus is live. Its shape also stops the plug being inserted wrongly.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The wire used in a fuse should have:

options.A: A very high melting point so that it never breaks
options.B: Magnetic properties so it can switch off the circuit
options.C: A very low resistance and a high thermal tolerance
options.D: A low melting point, so it melts when excess current flows

questions.explanation: A fuse is a deliberate weak link: its low-melting-point wire heats and melts when the current exceeds the rated value, breaking the circuit and protecting the apparatus and patient.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The earth wire of a mains cable is conventionally coloured:
questions.explanation: Earth is green/yellow, live is brown (formerly red) and neutral is blue (formerly black). The earth wire connects the metal casing of the apparatus to earth.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: A device used to regulate (vary) the current in a circuit by altering its resistance is called a:
questions.explanation: A rheostat is a variable resistor. Changing its resistance changes the current flowing in the circuit (Ohm's law, I = V/R).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Conversion of alternating current into direct (unidirectional) current is called rectification and is achieved with a:
questions.explanation: A diode conducts in one direction only, so it removes one half of an AC cycle (half-wave) or, in a bridge, inverts it (full-wave) to produce unidirectional current.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: According to Ohm's law, the current flowing through a conductor at constant temperature is:

options.A: Directly proportional to the potential difference and inversely proportional to the resistance
options.B: Inversely proportional to the potential difference
options.D: Directly proportional to both the resistance and the potential difference

questions.explanation: Ohm's law: I = V/R. For a given voltage, increasing the resistance reduces the current.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Joule's law states that the heat produced in a conductor is proportional to:

options.B: The voltage divided by the time
options.C: The square of the current, the resistance and the time (I²Rt)
options.D: The square of the resistance and the current

questions.explanation: Heat = I² × R × t. This is why a high-resistance skin interface heats under electrodes and why doubling the current quadruples the heating.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: A capacitor (condenser) is a device that:
questions.explanation: Two conducting plates separated by an insulator (dielectric) store charge. Capacitance C = Q/V.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The insulating (spacing) material between the plates of a capacitor is chosen to have:

options.D: A high dielectric constant, which increases the capacitance

questions.explanation: A higher dielectric constant allows a given plate area and spacing to store more charge, i.e. increases capacitance.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: In a step-up transformer:

options.A: The primary coil has more turns than the secondary coil
options.B: Direct current is stepped up with no change in turns
options.C: Primary and secondary have equal turns
options.D: The secondary coil has more turns than the primary coil

questions.explanation: Voltage across the secondary ∝ number of secondary turns. A step-up transformer has more secondary turns; it works only with changing (alternating) current.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Lenz's law states that:

options.A: Radiation intensity falls with the square of the distance
options.B: An induced EMF acts in a direction that opposes the change producing it
options.D: Heat produced is proportional to current squared

questions.explanation: The induced EMF always opposes the change in magnetic flux that causes it — the basis of self-inductance in coils and choke coils.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The instrument used to measure the intensity of current in a circuit is a/an:
questions.explanation: An ammeter measures current and has very low resistance, so it is connected in series. A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: An unknown electrical resistance can be determined with a:
questions.explanation: The Wheatstone bridge balances two ratio arms against a known and an unknown resistance, so the unknown value can be calculated when the galvanometer reads zero.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Skin resistance to an applied current is LOWERED by:

options.B: Using a very low-frequency current only

questions.explanation: Unlike metals, body tissues are ionic conductors; warming and moistening reduce skin resistance. Dry, cold, hairy skin presents higher impedance.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Why do medium-frequency currents pass through the skin more comfortably than low-frequency currents?

options.B: Skin capacitive reactance falls as frequency rises, so skin impedance is lower
options.C: They are not conducted by nerves at all
options.D: Skin resistance rises as frequency rises

questions.explanation: Skin behaves partly as a capacitor. Capacitive reactance = 1/(2πfC), so at higher frequencies the impedance is lower and more current penetrates with less discomfort at the skin.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The FIRST step in managing a patient or colleague who is still in contact with a live electrical source is to:

options.A: Wait for the person to let go on their own
options.C: Switch off the supply at the mains (or safely break contact with a non-conducting object)
options.D: Pull the person away with bare hands

questions.explanation: Touching a victim still in contact would pass current to the rescuer. Isolate the supply first, then assess breathing/circulation and start CPR if needed.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: A choke coil (inductor) in a circuit mainly:

options.A: Opposes rapid changes in current, allowing low-frequency/steady current but impeding high-frequency alternating current
options.B: Blocks direct current and passes only high frequencies

questions.explanation: An inductor's reactance rises with frequency (X = 2πfL), so it smooths current and attenuates high-frequency components.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The resting membrane potential of a typical peripheral nerve fibre is about:
questions.explanation: At rest the inside of a nerve fibre is about 70 mV negative relative to the outside. Skeletal muscle fibres rest nearer −90 mV.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The resting membrane potential of a skeletal muscle fibre is approximately:
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle fibres have a resting potential of about −90 mV, more negative than the −70 mV of nerve.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The transmitter chemical released at the neuromuscular junction is:
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine released from the motor nerve terminal binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate to depolarise the muscle fibre.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Which statement about peripheral nerve fibres is correct?

options.A: Conduction velocity is unrelated to fibre diameter
options.B: Unmyelinated C fibres conduct faster than A fibres
options.C: Small-diameter fibres have the lowest threshold to electrical stimulation
options.D: Large-diameter myelinated fibres conduct fastest and have the lowest stimulation threshold

questions.explanation: Large myelinated fibres (Aα/Aβ) are excited first and conduct fastest. This is why sensory TENS and motor stimulation can be selectively recruited before pain fibres.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Compared with voluntary contraction, electrically stimulated muscle contraction tends to recruit motor units:

options.A: Randomly with no relation to fibre size
options.B: In a reverse (non-selective) order, with large, fast-fatiguing units recruited first
options.C: In the same order, smallest first

questions.explanation: Large-diameter axons have the lowest electrical threshold, so large fast (type II) units are activated first; this is the reverse of the size principle and explains early fatigue with electrical stimulation.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The reaction produced beneath the cathode when direct current is passed through the tissues is:
questions.explanation: Under the cathode (−) sodium hydroxide forms → alkaline reaction, which is more irritant and liquefies tissue. Under the anode (+) hydrochloric acid forms → acidic reaction, which hardens tissue.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: During galvanic (direct) current application, excitability of the nerve is increased beneath the:
questions.explanation: The cathode partially depolarises the nerve, increasing excitability (catelectrotonus). The anode hyperpolarises and reduces excitability (anelectrotonus).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The weakest current intensity that produces a minimal visible muscle contraction when applied for an indefinitely long pulse duration is called:
questions.explanation: Rheobase is the minimum intensity (of a long-duration stimulus) that evokes a threshold response. Chronaxie is the pulse duration needed at twice the rheobase.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Chronaxie is defined as the:

options.A: Longest pulse duration the muscle can tolerate
options.C: Intensity required for a 1 ms pulse
options.D: Shortest pulse duration needed to excite the tissue at an intensity of twice the rheobase

questions.explanation: Chronaxie is a measure of tissue excitability; it is much longer in denervated muscle than in normal innervated muscle.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Which type of impulse is able to stimulate denervated muscle selectively while avoiding stimulation of surrounding normal innervated muscle and sensory nerves?

options.B: A short-duration, rapidly rising faradic pulse
options.C: A slowly rising, long-duration (e.g. triangular or trapezoidal) pulse

questions.explanation: Normal nerve accommodates to slowly rising currents and does not fire, whereas denervated muscle fibres have lost the ability to accommodate and respond to slow-rising, long-duration pulses.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Low-frequency currents used in electrotherapy have frequencies of approximately:
questions.explanation: Low frequency: up to ~1000 Hz. Medium frequency: 1000–10,000 Hz (e.g. interferential, Russian). High frequency: above 10 kHz (shortwave, microwave).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Medium-frequency currents have a frequency of:
questions.explanation: Interferential and Russian currents are medium-frequency currents (typically carrier 2000–4000 Hz).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: A pulse that has two opposite phases (one positive and one negative) within a single pulse is termed:
questions.explanation: Monophasic pulses deviate to one side of the baseline; biphasic pulses have both a positive and negative phase. Symmetrical biphasic pulses have no net polarity.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The classic faradic-type current used to stimulate normal innervated muscle consists of:

options.B: Short-duration (<1 ms) pulses repeated at about 50–100 per second
options.C: Long-duration pulses (>100 ms) repeated once per second

questions.explanation: Faradic-type current uses short pulses to stimulate the motor nerve, producing tetanic contraction at 50–100 Hz. It is unsuitable for denervated muscle.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Interrupted direct current of long pulse duration is used mainly to stimulate:

options.A: Nerve roots for pain gate control

questions.explanation: Denervated muscle has a higher chronaxie and needs long-duration pulses (tens to hundreds of ms) of adequate intensity to contract.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The ‘Russian current’ used for strengthening muscle is characterised by:

options.C: A direct current delivered in 100 ms pulses
options.D: A 2500 Hz medium-frequency carrier delivered in 50 bursts per second

questions.explanation: Kots’ Russian stimulation is a 2500 Hz sine carrier interrupted into 10 ms bursts (50 per second, 50% duty cycle), used to strengthen normal muscle.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Diadynamic currents (Bernard) are derived from:

options.A: Rectified 50 Hz mains sine waves (half-wave MF at 50 Hz and full-wave DF at 100 Hz)
options.B: Alternating current of 4000 Hz and 4100 Hz

questions.explanation: Diadynamic currents use half- or full-wave rectified sinusoids — MF (monophasé fixé, 50 Hz), DF (diphasé fixé, 100 Hz), CP, LP and RS modulations. They are unidirectional with a galvanic component.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Which current is described as having a prominent polarity effect and is therefore suited to iontophoresis and wound healing?
questions.explanation: Polarity effects require unidirectional current with a net charge. Symmetrical biphasic currents have no net DC and no polarity effects.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: High-voltage pulsed current (HVPC) is best described as:

options.A: A symmetrical biphasic square wave of long duration
options.B: A continuous direct current of low voltage
options.C: A twin-peak, monophasic pulse of very short duration with a low average current

questions.explanation: HVPC has a very high peak voltage (>150 V) but very short pulses (about 5–20 µs), so the average current is small and comfortable; it is used for oedema, wound healing and pain.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: In interferential therapy the therapeutic low-frequency effect is produced:

options.A: At the skin surface by a single low-frequency current
options.B: Within the tissues, where two medium-frequency currents of slightly different frequency interfere
options.C: Only when direct current is used
options.D: By the heat of the electrodes

questions.explanation: Two medium-frequency currents (e.g. 4000 Hz and 4100 Hz) cross in the tissues, producing an amplitude-modulated beat at the difference frequency (100 Hz) deep to the skin with less skin discomfort.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: A true interference pattern (endogenous IFT) in the tissues requires:

options.A: A quadripolar electrode arrangement with the two circuits crossing at the target
options.C: A single large and small electrode
options.D: A bipolar arrangement with premodulated current

questions.explanation: In quadripolar technique two separate circuits cross; the interference occurs within the tissue. In bipolar mode the current is premodulated within the machine, so no true interference occurs in the tissue.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Which IFT mode is selected to treat a diffuse area of pathology?

options.B: Single-frequency fixed mode with one electrode pair

questions.explanation: Scanning (‘vector’) mode rotates the interference field so the treatment covers a wider and less well-defined area.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: For pain relief through the gate-control mechanism, the beat frequency of IFT is usually set at about:
questions.explanation: High beat frequencies (~80–100 Hz) favour the segmental gate mechanism; low frequencies (2–10 Hz) favour endorphin-mediated pain relief and muscle contraction.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Conventional TENS is characterised by:

options.A: High frequency (~50–100 Hz) and low (sensory) intensity
options.B: Low frequency and high intensity producing muscle twitches
options.D: Direct current at a very low frequency

questions.explanation: Conventional TENS stimulates large Aβ fibres to activate the pain gate; patients feel a comfortable paraesthesia without muscle contraction.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Acupuncture-like TENS differs from conventional TENS in that it uses:

options.A: Low frequency (2–4 Hz) with high intensity producing visible muscle twitching, acting via endogenous opioids
options.B: Very high frequency with sensory-only intensity

questions.explanation: Low-rate, strong stimulation releases beta-endorphin and encephalins; analgesia has a slower onset but longer duration than conventional TENS.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: TENS should NOT be applied:

options.A: For post-operative wound pain at a distance from the wound
options.B: Over the carotid sinus or in a patient with a demand-type cardiac pacemaker
options.D: For pain in labour on the lower back

questions.explanation: Absolute cautions for TENS: demand pacemakers, over the carotid sinus, over the anterior neck, eyes, pregnant uterus (except back in labour), and areas of impaired sensation or thrombosis.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The quantity of ions delivered by iontophoresis is chiefly determined by the:

options.A: Current intensity multiplied by treatment time (mA·min)

questions.explanation: Faraday’s law: the amount of substance transported is proportional to the charge passed, i.e. current × time. Typical doses are 40–80 mA·min.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Which ion is delivered from the negative electrode (cathode) to soften adherent scar tissue?
questions.explanation: Chloride is negatively charged and repelled from the cathode; used for scar and adhesions. Acetate (negative) is used for calcific deposits. Zinc and lidocaine are positive ions delivered from the anode.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Acetic acid iontophoresis for calcific tendinitis relies on delivering which ion?
questions.explanation: Acetate is an anion; like charges repel, so it is driven into tissue from the cathode, where it may help dissolve calcium deposits.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: In a complete lesion of the motor nerve the strength-duration curve:

options.A: Shifts to the right and upward with no kink, and chronaxie is prolonged
options.B: Shows two kinks only in innervated muscle

questions.explanation: A denervated muscle needs longer pulse durations and higher intensities, so the curve moves right and up; a kink indicates partial denervation. The curve helps judge the degree of denervation.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: A characteristic finding in reaction of degeneration on galvanic testing is:

options.A: Absent response to direct current in all cases
options.B: Cathodal closing contraction much greater than anodal closing contraction with brisk response
options.C: Polarity reversal — anodal closing contraction becomes equal to or greater than cathodal closing contraction

questions.explanation: In normal muscle CCC > ACC with brisk twitches. In RD, contraction is sluggish (vermicular), faradic response is lost and ACC ≥ CCC (polarity reversal).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Insertional activity on needle EMG is seen in:

options.D: Normal innervated muscle (a brief burst on needle movement)

questions.explanation: Normal muscle shows brief insertional activity lasting less than a second, followed by electrical silence at rest.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Spontaneous fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves at rest on EMG, appearing about 2–3 weeks after injury, indicate:
questions.explanation: Denervated muscle fibres become hypersensitive to acetylcholine and fire spontaneously; fibrillations and positive sharp waves are the typical findings at rest.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: An EMG motor unit potential is termed polyphasic when it has:

options.B: No phases but only a baseline

questions.explanation: Normal motor unit potentials are bi- or triphasic (up to four phases). Polyphasic potentials occur in reinnervation (long, large) and in myopathy (short, small).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The classical needle-EMG finding in a primary myopathy is:

options.A: Short-duration, low-amplitude polyphasic motor unit potentials with early full recruitment
options.B: Fasciculations as the only abnormal finding
options.C: Giant, long-duration motor unit potentials with reduced recruitment
options.D: Complete electrical silence on voluntary effort

questions.explanation: In myopathy muscle fibres drop out from each motor unit, so potentials become small and brief; many units are needed for little force, giving early recruitment.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The normal motor nerve conduction velocity in the upper limb is approximately:
questions.explanation: Upper limb motor conduction velocity is typically 50–70 m/s; lower limb values are lower (about 40–50 m/s) and decrease with cooling and age.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The H-reflex is clinically used to assess conduction through:

options.A: The S1 root (via the tibial nerve to soleus)
options.C: The C5 root via musculocutaneous nerve

questions.explanation: The H-reflex is the electrical analogue of the ankle jerk: a monosynaptic reflex through the S1 segment. A delayed or absent H-reflex suggests S1 radiculopathy or neuropathy.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Transfer of heat through a fluid such as moving water or air is called:
questions.explanation: Convection is heat transfer by movement of fluid; conduction is by direct contact; radiation by electromagnetic waves; evaporation takes latent heat from the surface.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: During exercise in a hot, humid environment the principal mechanism of body heat loss is:
questions.explanation: Evaporation is the main route of heat loss during exercise; it becomes ineffective in high humidity, raising the risk of heat illness.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The energy absorbed or released when a substance changes state without a change in temperature is called:
questions.explanation: Latent heat is the energy needed for a change of state (e.g. water to vapour); it explains the cooling effect of vapocoolant sprays and evaporation.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Van't Hoff's law relates to the therapeutic effect of heat by stating that:

options.A: The rate of a chemical reaction (metabolic rate) increases about two to three times for each 10 °C rise in temperature
options.C: Absorbed radiation produces a chemical change only when it penetrates
options.D: Heat produced is proportional to current squared

questions.explanation: Van't Hoff's law underlies the increase in tissue metabolism with heating, which increases demand for oxygen and promotes repair.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Which tissue has the LOWEST thermal conductivity and so insulates the underlying tissues from superficial heat?
questions.explanation: Fat is a poor conductor; heat applied to a thick fatty layer penetrates less, and is retained within the fat, increasing the risk of superficial burns.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: A hot (hydrocollator) pack is applied with several layers of towelling between the pack and the skin mainly to:

options.A: Prevent burns by insulating the skin from excessive heat
options.B: Increase the temperature of the pack
options.C: Reduce the specific heat of water

questions.explanation: Towel layers (6–8) insulate the skin and let the heat build up gradually; the patient should never lie on the pack.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: A paraffin wax bath is particularly suitable for:

options.A: Deep heating of the hip joint
options.D: Painful stiff small joints of the hands in rheumatoid arthritis

questions.explanation: Wax gives comfortable conductive heat in a layered glove over irregular surfaces such as the hand, relieving pain and stiffness; it is contraindicated over open wounds and in impaired sensation.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: In a wax bath, paraffin wax is commonly mixed with liquid paraffin (mineral oil) in the ratio:
questions.explanation: Seven parts wax to one part liquid paraffin lowers the melting point to about 54 °C, so a tolerable temperature produces a skin-conforming coating.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: A paraffin wax bath at about 50–55 °C does not usually burn the patient because wax has:

options.A: A low specific heat and low thermal conductivity

questions.explanation: Wax has a low specific heat and is a poor conductor, so only a small amount of heat is transferred to the skin; a thin layer solidifies and insulates.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Fluidotherapy is a form of:

options.C: Dry heat using a warm air-suspended bed of fine particles

questions.explanation: Fluidotherapy circulates warm air through finely divided cellulose particles that behave like a fluid, giving dry heat with massage-like stimulation.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: A contrast bath in the upper or lower limb is traditionally applied as:

options.D: About 3–4 minutes of warm immersion alternating with about 1 minute of cold

questions.explanation: Alternating vasodilatation and vasoconstriction (the ‘pump’ effect) is thought to help in subacute oedema and stiffness; the usual ratio is 4:1 hot:cold.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Superficial heat should be avoided over:

options.C: A stiff, painful but normally sensate hand
options.D: Areas of impaired skin sensation or impaired circulation

questions.explanation: Burns result when the patient cannot sense or respond to excessive heat; other cautions are acute inflammation, bleeding and malignancy.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Infrared radiation lies in the electromagnetic spectrum:

options.A: At a shorter wavelength than ultraviolet
options.D: Between visible light and microwaves (about 700 nm to 1 mm)

questions.explanation: Infrared has longer wavelengths than visible red light. Therapeutically, 750 nm – 400,000 nm is commonly quoted.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Compared with non-luminous infrared generators, luminous generators:

options.C: Emit longer wavelengths absorbed in the outer epidermis only
options.D: Emit shorter-wavelength IR that penetrates a little deeper, along with visible light, and need no warm-up

questions.explanation: Luminous IR lamps (filament lamps) emit visible and near-IR radiation (to ~ 5–10 mm); non-luminous generators use heated elements, emit longer wavelengths absorbed superficially and require 5–10 minutes to warm up.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The inverse square law states that the intensity of radiation at a surface is:

options.B: Inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source
options.D: Proportional to the square of the distance

questions.explanation: Doubling the distance of an IR or UV lamp reduces the intensity to one quarter, which is why lamp distance must be measured and reproduced.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: According to Lambert's cosine law, absorption of radiation at a surface is maximal when the rays strike it:

options.D: At right angles (perpendicular) to the surface

questions.explanation: Maximum intensity is received when the beam is perpendicular to the surface; reduces with the cosine of the angle of incidence.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The Grotthus–Draper law states that:

options.A: Radiation intensity falls with the square of the distance
options.B: Metabolic rate doubles for each 10 °C rise
options.C: Only radiation that is absorbed by the tissue can produce an effect in it
options.D: Heat produced is proportional to I²Rt

questions.explanation: For any physiological effect, radiation must be absorbed; reflected or transmitted radiation produces no effect.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The most commonly used frequency for therapeutic shortwave diathermy (SWD) is:
questions.explanation: SWD uses 27.12 MHz (11 m); 13.56 MHz and 40.68 MHz are also allocated. 2450 MHz belongs to microwave diathermy.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The word ‘diathermy’ literally means:
questions.explanation: Dia = through, therme = heat. It denotes deep heating of tissue by high-frequency currents.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: In the capacitor-field method of SWD the tissues are placed between two electrodes and the dominant heating effect is in tissues of:

options.B: Low impedance such as muscle only
options.D: High impedance such as fat and superficial structures

questions.explanation: In an electric field, heating is greatest in tissues with high resistance (fat, skin), so the capacitor-field method heats subcutaneous fat first; in the inductive method, high-conductivity tissue (muscle) heats more via eddy currents.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: In the inductive (cable/coil) method of SWD, heat is primarily produced by:

options.B: Eddy currents induced in tissues of high conductivity such as muscle

questions.explanation: A coil carrying high-frequency current creates a changing magnetic field that induces eddy currents in tissues with a high water and ion content.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: To achieve deep heating by the capacitor-field method the electrodes are placed:

options.A: Side by side on the same surface (coplanar)
options.B: Directly on bare skin with no spacing
options.C: On opposite sides of the part (contraplanar)
options.D: One electrode on the skin and the other on the wall

questions.explanation: Contraplanar placement makes the field pass through the part, treating deeper tissues; coplanar placement is used for superficial lesions.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: If different-sized electrodes are used in the coplanar method, the heating effect is:

options.B: Concentrated under the smaller electrode, where field density is higher

questions.explanation: A smaller electrode gives a higher field density, hence more heating beneath it. Equal-sized electrodes give an even distribution.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: In SWD the spacing between the electrode and the skin should be made of material with:

options.B: A high dielectric constant such as water
options.D: A low dielectric constant (e.g. air, felt or foam)

questions.explanation: Spacers of low dielectric constant (air, felt) ensure the field spreads into the tissue and avoid concentrating heat in the superficial fat.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: SWD should NOT be applied to a patient with:

options.C: A cardiac pacemaker or metal implants in the field

questions.explanation: Metal implants and pacemakers concentrate or are disturbed by the field; other contraindications include pregnancy, malignancy, impaired circulation or sensation, haemorrhage, and moisture over the field.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The thermal effect of pulsed shortwave diathermy becomes evident when the mean power output exceeds about:
questions.explanation: Pulsed SWD with a mean power under about 5 W is considered athermal; above this level heating occurs. Pulsed energy is chosen for acute conditions.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The frequency of microwave diathermy used therapeutically is:
questions.explanation: Microwaves occupy 300 MHz–30 GHz; therapeutic units use 2450 MHz (12.25 cm), 915 MHz or 433.9 MHz.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Microwaves for diathermy are generated by a:
questions.explanation: A magnetron produces the very high frequencies required; waves are radiated by a directed emitter.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Microwave energy is absorbed MOST by tissues with a:

options.D: High water content, such as muscle

questions.explanation: Water molecules absorb microwaves strongly, so muscle heats preferentially; fat and bone are heated less.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Which structure requires special protection during microwave diathermy near the head?
questions.explanation: The lens of the eye has little blood flow to dissipate heat; microwave exposure can cause cataract, so patients need protective goggles and the eyes must be avoided.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Therapeutic ultrasound is produced by the:

options.A: Reverse piezoelectric effect in a crystal

questions.explanation: An alternating voltage applied to a piezoelectric crystal (quartz, barium titanate, lead zirconate titanate) makes it vibrate at the same frequency, producing sound waves.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The frequencies commonly used in therapeutic ultrasound are:
questions.explanation: 1 MHz penetrates deeper (about 3–5 cm); 3 MHz is absorbed in the superficial 1–2 cm.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Compared with 1 MHz ultrasound, 3 MHz ultrasound is:

options.C: Absorbed deeper and used for the hip joint
options.D: Absorbed more superficially and used for shallow structures

questions.explanation: Absorption increases with frequency; therefore 3 MHz is attenuated more rapidly and suits superficial tendons and joints.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Ultrasound intensity is expressed in:
questions.explanation: Intensity = power (W) / effective radiating area (cm²). Typical therapeutic range is 0.1–2.0 W/cm².
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: A pulsed ultrasound output with a duty cycle of 20% corresponds to a mark : space ratio of:
questions.explanation: Duty cycle = on time / (on + off) = 1/(1+4) = 20%. A 1:1 ratio is a 50% duty cycle.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: A coupling medium (gel) is used with the ultrasound transducer in order to:

options.A: Increase the heat of the gel
options.C: Reflect the ultrasound back into the machine
options.D: Eliminate air between the transducer and the skin so the energy is transmitted

questions.explanation: Air reflects almost all ultrasound; gel (or water) ensures acoustic contact.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: When treating an irregular surface such as the ankle with the underwater technique, the transducer is held:

options.B: About 1–2 cm from the skin, with no contact and moved slowly
options.C: In firm contact with the skin
options.D: On the far wall of the tank

questions.explanation: The transducer is kept close to but not touching the skin; the treated part and transducer are both in degassed water. Bubbles must be wiped off the skin.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The decrease in intensity of an ultrasound beam as it travels through tissue, due to absorption and scattering, is termed:
questions.explanation: Attenuation = absorption + scattering (+ reflection) of the beam; higher frequencies are attenuated more.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Unidirectional movement of fluid along the surface of a cell membrane caused by the ultrasound field is called:
questions.explanation: Acoustic streaming can alter membrane permeability and stimulate repair; it is the main non-thermal mechanism and the basis of phonophoresis.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Cavitation in ultrasound refers to the:

options.A: Reflection of the beam from bone
options.D: Formation and oscillation of gas bubbles in tissue fluids

questions.explanation: Stable cavitation (bubbles oscillating) is useful non-thermally; transient (unstable) cavitation, where bubbles collapse, is damaging and must be avoided.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The proportion of ultrasound energy reflected at an interface between two media depends mainly on:

options.A: The frequency of the mains supply
options.C: The temperature of the transducer only
options.D: The difference in acoustic impedance of the two media

questions.explanation: The greater the difference in acoustic impedance, the greater the reflection — almost total at an air–tissue interface and high at a soft tissue–bone interface (periosteal burning risk).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Which tissue absorbs ultrasound energy MOST per unit thickness?

options.D: Bone and other tissues rich in collagen and protein

questions.explanation: Absorption is highest in tissues with high protein/collagen content such as bone, tendon and ligament; lowest in fluid and fat.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The ratio of the spatial peak intensity to the spatial average intensity of an ultrasound beam is called the:
questions.explanation: BNR describes how evenly power is distributed over the transducer face; a lower BNR (ideally < 6:1) is safer, avoiding hot spots.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The length of the near field (Fresnel zone) of an ultrasound beam increases when:

options.C: The transducer radius is larger or the wavelength is shorter (higher frequency)

questions.explanation: Near-field length = r²/λ. Within the near field the beam is highly irregular; the far field is more uniform and divergent.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound is preferred over continuous ultrasound in the:

options.A: Treatment of verrucae using high-power continuous output
options.B: Acute stage of soft tissue injury or for fracture healing, when heating is undesirable
options.C: Chronic muscle contracture, to maximise heating
options.D: Deep cervical muscle spasm in obese patients

questions.explanation: Pulsed ultrasound delivers non-thermal effects (streaming, cavitation) with minimal heating and is suited to acute inflammation and bone repair.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Therapeutic ultrasound should NOT be applied over:

options.A: A chronic tendinopathy of the supraspinatus
options.B: A healing ligament sprain in the subacute phase
options.C: A muscle contracture with intact sensation
options.D: A pregnant uterus, the eyes, or a known malignant tumour

questions.explanation: Ultrasound is contraindicated over the pregnant uterus, eyes, testes, malignancy, thrombophlebitis and areas of impaired circulation or sensation; also with caution over growing epiphyses and pacemakers.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Phonophoresis is the use of ultrasound to:

options.A: Reduce skin resistance to direct current
options.B: Drive a topical drug through the skin into underlying tissue
options.C: Remove a drug from the blood

questions.explanation: Phonophoresis uses acoustic streaming and increased membrane permeability to deliver topical agents such as hydrocortisone or NSAIDs.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Sound waves with a frequency below about 20 Hz are called:
questions.explanation: Infrasound < 20 Hz; audible 20 Hz – 20 kHz; ultrasound > 20 kHz.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The wavelength range of UVB is:
questions.explanation: UVA 315–400 nm; UVB 280–315 nm; UVC 100–280 nm. UVB is the main erythemogenic and vitamin D–forming band.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Which band of ultraviolet radiation has a strong germicidal action and is filtered out by the ozone layer?
questions.explanation: UVC (about 254 nm) is bactericidal and absorbed by atmospheric ozone; it penetrates only the stratum corneum.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Vitamin D synthesis in the skin results from exposure to:
questions.explanation: 7-dehydrocholesterol in the skin is converted by UVB into cholecalciferol (vitamin D3).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The minimal erythema dose (first-degree erythema, E1) is the:

options.A: Dose that has no effect at all
options.B: Smallest UV exposure that produces just-visible reddening of the skin after the latent period
options.D: Dose that causes immediate tanning only

questions.explanation: E1 is the threshold dose. E2 ≈ 2.5 × E1 (bright red, peeling), E3 ≈ 5 × E1 (painful with blisters/oedema), E4 ≈ 10 × E1 (severe blistering).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: For an effective erythema reaction on skin that has become thickened and pigmented from previous UV exposure, the next dose should be:

options.A: Increased to overcome the protective thickening and tolerance
options.B: Delivered with the lamp at double the distance
options.D: Kept the same, since tolerance never develops

questions.explanation: Repeated exposures produce epidermal thickening (acanthosis) and pigmentation, so tolerance develops and doses must be increased (e.g. by 25–75%) to maintain the same erythema.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Erythema after UVB exposure is mainly due to:

options.B: Release of vasodilator chemicals (histamine-like substances, prostaglandins) from damaged epidermal cells

questions.explanation: UV damages keratinocytes, releasing vasoactive substances that dilate dermal capillaries after a latent period (hours).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Skin cancer risk after long-term ultraviolet exposure is mainly attributed to:

options.C: DNA damage and the immunosuppressive effect of UV

questions.explanation: UVB causes pyrimidine dimers in DNA and suppresses local immunity; cumulative exposure increases risk of squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma and melanoma.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Which lamp is the best choice to irradiate a small, localised area such as a sinus or a cavity?

options.C: A water-cooled Kromayer lamp with a quartz applicator

questions.explanation: The Kromayer lamp is a water-cooled mercury vapour lamp whose UV is directed through a quartz applicator in contact with the tissue, allowing treatment of sinuses, cavities and small ulcers.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: A Theraktin tunnel (bank of fluorescent tubes) is used for:

options.A: General (whole-body or large-area) UV irradiation, e.g. in psoriasis

questions.explanation: The Theraktin tunnel is a semi-circular cradle of long-wave UV fluorescent tubes giving general irradiation; it is used for conditions such as psoriasis often with coal tar (Leeds regimen).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: In PUVA therapy for psoriasis, UVA irradiation is given:

options.B: At the same time as an X-ray

questions.explanation: Psoralen photosensitises the skin; UVA is then given about 2 hours after ingestion. Eye protection (UV-blocking glasses) is needed for many hours afterwards.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: In psoriasis the epidermal transit time is shortened to about:
questions.explanation: Normal epidermal turnover takes about 28 days (up to 70 including full migration); in psoriasis it is greatly accelerated; UV reduces cell proliferation.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: To stimulate healing in a clean indolent ulcer or pressure sore with UV, the dose commonly applied is:

options.B: A high erythemal dose, e.g. E3–E4, to the margins and base

questions.explanation: High erythema doses cause exfoliation of necrotic tissue and stimulate granulation. Infected wounds require UVC/short UV with higher dosage.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The latent period between UV exposure and the appearance of erythema is:

options.A: Longer for UVA than for UVB; typically about 2–8 hours (UVB)
options.B: Longer for a higher dose in every case

questions.explanation: UVB erythema appears after a latent period of about 1.5–8 h, peaks at 12–24 h, and the greater the dose the shorter the latent period.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The word LASER stands for:

options.A: Light Amplitude of Strong Electrical Rays
options.B: Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation

questions.explanation: A laser produces an intense, coherent beam through stimulated emission of photons.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: A laser beam is characterised by being:
questions.explanation: The three classical properties of laser light: single wavelength (monochromatic), in-phase waves (coherent) and non-divergent (collimated).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Population inversion in laser physics refers to a state in which:

options.A: More electrons are in the ground state than in the excited state
options.B: The medium is at absolute zero
options.C: More electrons are in an excited (metastable) state than in the ground state
options.D: All electrons are removed from the atom

questions.explanation: Population inversion is required for stimulated emission to exceed absorption and thereby amplify light.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The wavelength of a helium–neon (He–Ne) laser is about:
questions.explanation: The He–Ne laser emits visible red light at 632.8 nm with shallow penetration (~ 0.5–2 mm), used for superficial wounds.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Compared with the He–Ne laser, infrared diode lasers (e.g. 830–904 nm):
questions.explanation: Near-infrared wavelengths are absorbed less by haemoglobin and melanin, so penetrate deeper (up to a few centimetres).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The dose (energy density) delivered in laser therapy is expressed in:
questions.explanation: Dose (J/cm²) = power density (W/cm²) × time (s). Power is in watts, a rate of energy delivery (J/s).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The most important safety precaution while using a therapeutic laser is to:

options.A: Protect the eyes of the patient and operator with wavelength-specific goggles
options.B: Apply the laser to the eyes for 30 seconds
options.C: Treat in a dark, reflective room
options.D: Cover the machine with a wet towel

questions.explanation: Laser light can damage the retina even at low powers; goggles rated for the wavelength must be worn and reflective surfaces avoided.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The immediate response of cutaneous blood vessels to application of ice is:

options.C: A rise in blood pressure only

questions.explanation: Cold causes reflex and direct vasoconstriction, reducing blood flow, oedema formation and metabolism.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: The alternating vasoconstriction and vasodilatation that occurs in the skin when cold is applied for a prolonged period is called:
questions.explanation: Prolonged cold causes cold-induced vasodilatation every few minutes to protect tissue from freezing; this limits the benefit of very long applications.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Cryotherapy is used to temporarily reduce spasticity because it:

options.B: Lowers nerve conduction velocity and muscle spindle firing

questions.explanation: Cooling decreases afferent firing and conduction velocity, lowering tone for a short period during which stretching or exercise can be performed.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: To avoid the reactive vasodilatation phase, a standard ice pack application is usually limited to:
questions.explanation: 10–15 minutes reduces tissue temperature effectively; longer exposure risks nerve injury and tissue damage.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: In the immediate management of acute soft tissue injury, RICE stands for:
questions.explanation: RICE limits bleeding and oedema. Many protocols now add Protection and avoid anti-inflammatory heat in the first 48–72 hours.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Which statement about the effects of cooling is FALSE?

options.C: Motor skill performance and muscle strength improve immediately after cooling

questions.explanation: After prolonged cooling, strength, speed and dexterity are temporarily reduced; performance should be assessed before heavy training or skilled activity.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Cryotherapy is contraindicated in:

options.C: Raynaud's disease and cold hypersensitivity (cold urticaria)

questions.explanation: Cold may provoke vasospasm in Raynaud's disease and release of histamine in cold urticaria; avoid it also in impaired sensation and arterial insufficiency.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Traction applied with a light weight for a prolonged period (hours) is:
questions.explanation: Continuous traction uses small forces for long periods (e.g. in bed rest to rest an area); intermittent traction alternates higher force with rest periods for 10–30 minutes.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Mechanical cervical traction to separate the posterior elements (e.g. facet joints, foramen) is usually applied with the neck positioned in:
questions.explanation: Moderate flexion opens the intervertebral foramina and posterior joints most effectively; extension would compress them.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: Which condition is a contraindication to lumbar or cervical traction?

options.B: Mechanical low back pain with muscle spasm
options.D: Mild lumbar disc protrusion without neurological deficit

questions.explanation: Traction is contraindicated with cord signs, unstable fracture, severe osteoporosis, infection, malignancy, vertebrobasilar insufficiency and acute inflammatory arthritis (e.g. rheumatoid atlantoaxial instability).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy

questions.question: To produce measurable separation of lumbar vertebrae, the traction force needs to exceed approximately:
questions.explanation: Because of the friction of the body on the couch and the strength of the lumbar ligaments, forces of roughly 50% of body weight or more are needed for lumbar separation; lower forces (about 25%) are used for comfort and initial treatment.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy; facts cross-checked with Suraj Kumar, MCQs for MPT Entrance Examination (2nd ed.), Ch. 2 Electrotherapy
